topics: Inference from sample statistics, confidence intervals, and margin of error

body.en: Around 4–6 Digital SAT questions target statistics: reading distributions, choosing the right measure of center or spread, and interpreting survey results with a stated margin of error.

Mean (average) — pulled toward outliers. Median — middle value; resistant to outliers. Standard deviation — typical distance from the mean; the SAT asks you to compare or interpret SD, never to compute it. A histogram skewed right has mean > median; skewed left has mean < median.

Eight salaries (thousands): 30, 32, 35, 36, 37, 38, 40, 120.

Mean \(=368/8=46\). Median \(=(36+37)/2=36.5\).

The outlier (120) inflates the mean. The median better represents a typical salary.

Set A: {10,10,10,10}.  Set B: {4,8,12,16}. Both have mean 10.

Set A has SD = 0 (no spread). Set B has a larger SD because values vary around the mean.

A poll of 600 voters gives 54 % support with margin of error ±3 %.

The true population support is estimated between 51 % and 57 %. Since the entire interval exceeds 50 %, the data suggest majority support — but only for the population the sample represents.

label.en: ⚠️ SAT Traps & Pitfalls — Statistics, Sampling & Margin of Error

body.en:
• Margin of Error Depends on Sample Size, NOT Population: Increasing the sample size ($n$) reduces the margin of error (proportional to $1/\sqrt{n}$). The total population size has negligible impact on margin of error.
  • Generalization Boundaries: A random sample can only be generalized to the population from which the sample was drawn. A survey of visitors at an athletic store cannot generalize to all city residents.
  • Outlier Pull: Extreme high outliers pull the mean upward without significantly shifting the median ($\text{Mean} > \text{Median}$ for right-skewed data). For skewed data, the median and IQR are preferred over the mean and standard deviation.
  • Standard Deviation Definition: Standard deviation measures the spread or dispersion of values around the mean. Two datasets can have the same mean and range but very different standard deviations if values are clustered tightly vs. spread toward extremes.

label.en: Exam Practice 9.C — Skewness, Outliers & Measures of Center

body.en:
Question: A dataset consists of the salaries of 20 employees at a startup company. The salaries range from $50,000 to $90,000, with a mean of $68,000 and a median of $65,000. If the CEO joins the company with a salary of $1,200,000, which measure of center will increase by the greatest amount?

Solution: The CEO's salary is an extreme positive outlier ($1,200,000$). The mean is calculated by summing all values and dividing by 21, which will increase dramatically by $(1,200,000 - 68,000)/21 \approx \$53,900$. The median, being resistant to outliers, will simply shift to the next ranked value in the middle (increasing by at most a few thousand dollars). Therefore, the mean increases by the greatest amount.

question.en:
SAT-style Q1: Two data sets have the same mean of 50. Set A has standard deviation 2; Set B has standard deviation 8. Which is true?

(A) Set B values are closer to the mean.
(B) Set B has greater variability.
(C) The two sets have the same range.
(D) Set A has more data points.

solution.en: (B). A higher SD means values are, on average, farther from the mean — greater variability.

question.en:
SAT-style Q2: A school randomly samples 80 students; 60 % prefer longer lunches, margin of error ±5 %. Which conclusion is best?

(A) Exactly 60 % of all students prefer longer lunches.
(B) Between 55 % and 65 % of all students at the school prefer longer lunches.
(C) Results apply to all students nationwide.
(D) No conclusion can be drawn from the sample.

solution.en: (B). Random sample → generalise to the school. Margin of error creates the interval 60 % ± 5 % = 55 %–65 %. Not all students nationwide, so (C) is wrong.
